w1d1r6: A team can keep running without a PM because others quietly fill the gaps, so a PM has to earn their place through the results they create.
Raw intelligence comes first: a sharp, fast-learning candidate with little experience often beats an average one with many years in the role.
A technical background helps a PM win engineers' trust and explain detail to others, but former engineers must fully stop doing the engineering themselves.
Good PMs have strong product instincts: they spot problems early, notice great products others overlook and can teach you something about your own product.
PMs rarely have formal authority, so look for leadership earned through influence, the ability to speak for customers, engineering and sales at once, and a record of shipping a product end to end.
w1d1r7: A good PM takes full ownership and acts like the CEO of the product, judged by whether it succeeds. A bad PM keeps a list of reasons why things went wrong.
Good PMs define the 'what' and leave the 'how' to engineering. Bad PMs drift into project management or try to design the technical solution themselves.
Good PMs put direction in writing and take clear positions. Bad PMs offer opinions in passing and later claim they saw the problems coming.
Good PMs keep the team focused on customers and revenue and split big problems into smaller ones. Bad PMs chase feature counts and try to fix everything at once.

Good PMs define their own job and how success is measured, explain even the obvious clearly and stay disciplined about routine work like weekly status updates. The essay is from an earlier era of tech, so take the habits rather than every detail.
w1d1r2: Common myths: a PM is not a project manager, not a general manager, and not unrelated to technology. The 'mini-CEO' label really means a PM sits at the centre of business, technology and user experience.

In broad terms the PM does everything needed to ship a quality product: user and market research, business strategy and modelling, building a great user experience, getting it built technically, and taking it to market.

Step 1 is understanding the user (surveys, interviews, watching people use the product, analysing data) and the market, including what competitors offer. In B2B, knowing the competition can be the difference between winning and losing a sale.
Design the experience by prototyping, testing with real users and repeating until it fits. Then work with engineers to build and ship.
Building isn't the end: growth, sales collateral and even meeting key clients are part of the job. A PM must do all this without direct authority over anyone.
w1d1r3: Hard skills: a problem-solving attitude, enough tech understanding to know how products and systems talk to each other, deep user understanding, and a good eye for UX.
Business sense matters: a product users love still gets shut down if it doesn't support the company's business model and P&L.
Be analytical and data-driven, reading usage data to understand why users stay or leave and what to build next.
Soft skills: lead without authority (nobody reports to you), communicate clearly (especially in writing), and take feedback without taking it personally.
Ruthless prioritization: you'll always have more ideas than capacity, so focus on the few that matter most.
w1d1r4: PMs oversee the whole lifecycle of a product and work at the intersection of users (UX), business and technology. No coding is required.
Key responsibilities: empathy for users and advocating their needs, managing the build cycle (problem → ideas → experiments → launch), and bringing cross-functional teams together.
Entry-level titles to look for: Associate Product Manager (APM) or Product Associate. Mentorship mentioned in a job ad is a good sign for beginners.
Real job ads (HubSpot APM, TripAdvisor, Uber checkout) repeatedly ask for user empathy, cross-functional collaboration, problem solving, lifecycle ownership and metric tracking.
Roles vary in emphasis: some lean on UX, some on delivery, some on technical depth (e.g. platform/payments), so match ads to your background.
w1d1r5: There's no typical PM day. Work shifts with the product stage: discovery (user interviews), definition (MVP planning with design), execution (building with engineers, A/B tests with data science).
Mornings: triage urgent emails and messages, then check product health dashboards (north star and supporting metrics) and flag anything trending the wrong way.
Daily engineering stand-up (scrum) to unblock the team, clarify requirements and share updates like a new PRD.
Usability sessions to test newly shipped features and catch bugs, plus 1:1s with marketing, ML and data science counterparts.
End of day: focused solo work such as writing PRDs, reviewing other teams' docs and sending leadership updates. Much of a PM's job is meetings that unblock others.
w1d2r2: Product sense = consistently building products that have the intended impact on users. It rests on empathy (finding real needs) and creativity (solving them well). It's learned, not innate.
Examples: the original iPhone (aesthetics matter), Gmail (storage, search, threading) and Superhuman (speed for busy professionals) all came from spotting unmet needs.
Practice 1: regularly watch real people use products (yours and others) to spot subtle functional, social and emotional needs.
Practice 2: deconstruct everyday products. Ask why they were designed the way they are and what trade-offs were made.
Practices 3–4: learn from great product thinkers, and stay curious about changes in technology and your domain that open up new solutions.
w1d2r3: A product critique judges a product against what the user is trying to achieve, not personal taste or the designer's intent.
Start by asking who the product is for and what problem it solves, then walk through it as that user.
Look at it in stages: first impression, first use, and long-term use each reveal different problems.
Prioritize feedback in layers: first is it valuable (does it solve the problem?), then is it easy to use, then is it delightful. Leave visual polish for last.
Use outside signals such as app reviews and social media comments to check your view against real users.
w1d2r4: Product Hunt is a community site that features new tech products every day, ranked by upvotes and comments.
Use it to build product sense: browse daily launches and ask what problem each solves, for whom, and why it might win or fail.
Launch pages show how makers pitch their product (taglines, positioning, first-user feedback), which is useful for learning GTM and messaging.
Comment threads show real early-adopter reactions, feature requests and objections.
w1d2r5: First principles are basic truths that can't be broken down further. First-principles thinking means questioning every assumption instead of copying what others do.
Illustration: instead of seeing a motorboat, a tank and a bicycle, see their parts (motor, treads, skis, seat, handlebars) and recombine them into a snowmobile.
Step 1: clearly identify the problem (Einstein: spend most of your time understanding the problem).
Step 2: break it down to fundamentals, like a tree's trunk and branches before the leaves. Musk found battery materials cost about $80/kWh against $600/kWh battery packs.
Step 3: rebuild a new solution from those fundamentals, free of 'how it's always done' beliefs.
w1d2r6: Musk contrasts reasoning by analogy (doing things because others did them, with small iterations) with reasoning from first principles.
First principles is a physics approach: boil things down to the most fundamental truths you're sure of, then reason up from there. It takes more mental effort.
Analogy-based thinking would have said nobody wants cars because horses work fine. Past constraints aren't laws.

Battery example: packs cost $600/kWh historically, but the raw materials (cobalt, nickel, aluminium, carbon, polymers, a steel can) cost about $80/kWh on the metals market, so the gap is a design and manufacturing problem to solve.
w1d2r8: MECE ("mee-see") stands for Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive: group information so buckets don't overlap and together cover everything.
Example: splitting people into under 60 and 60+ is MECE. Splitting into under 60 and 50–70 is not (overlap, and gaps).
Consultants (McKinsey and other MBB firms) use it to break complex client problems into parts that can be analyzed one by one. Frameworks like Porter's Five Forces and the 4Cs are built on it.
Three MECE tools: issue trees (break a problem into sub-issues), decision trees (map choices and outcomes) and hypothesis trees (test likely answers).
Classic issue tree: 'Restaurant not profitable' → increase revenue (more orders, higher prices) vs reduce costs (salaries, rent, raw materials), with each branch broken down further.
w1d2r9: MECE means grouping ideas into buckets that are Mutually Exclusive (no overlap) and Collectively Exhaustive (nothing missing). It's expected in consulting case interviews.
Test: every item belongs to exactly one bucket, and the buckets cover all possibilities.
MECE frameworks include issue trees, decision trees and hypothesis trees, used to split big, messy problems into small, solvable ones.
Worked example: a profitability issue tree splits into revenue (number of orders × price) and costs (salary, rent, raw materials), then asks 'how?' at each level down to concrete actions.
w1d3r4: Product teams have two jobs that pull against each other: learning quickly what customers actually need, and shipping reliable software that customers can depend on.
Discovery is about gathering evidence that an idea is worth building. Delivery is about building it to production quality: scalable, tested, instrumented and maintainable.
Production engineering is the most expensive part of making a product, so spending it on an idea nobody has validated is the most common form of waste.
Many discovery techniques, such as testing prototypes with real users, need little or no engineering time and can be run with opt-in customers instead of public releases.
Run discovery and delivery as separate tracks: learn fast first, then hand validated ideas to engineers to build properly.
w1d3r5: Every product idea has to clear four risks: value (will people buy or use it), usability (can they figure it out), feasibility (can the team build it) and business viability (does it work for the business).
The PM owns value and viability risk, the product designer owns usability risk and the lead engineer owns feasibility risk.
Viability is about more than revenue: fit with sales and marketing, legal and partner constraints, the cost of acquiring customers and consistency with the brand all count.
Value risk is usually the hardest to retire, but a product customers love can still fail if it does not work for the business.
Strong teams tackle these risks early, before building, work on them together across product, design and engineering, and judge success by outcomes rather than features shipped.
w2d3r5: The Double Diamond (UK Design Council) shows design as a systematic process: define the right problem before finding the right solution.
Discover (diverge): explore by talking to and observing users and gathering insights into their needs, thoughts and feelings.
Define (converge): filter the insights down to the essence and reframe the core problem and scope.
Develop (diverge): generate as many ideas as possible, quantity over quality, in collaboration across disciplines and with users.
Deliver (converge): prototype the best ideas simply and test them with users. The process is iterative, with learning loops that raise the chance of success.
w1d3r1: The product life cycle runs from market introduction to removal from shelves, in four stages: introduction, growth, maturity, decline.
Introduction: heavy marketing spend to build awareness, low sales, little competition, and often losses.
Growth: sales and revenue climb, competitors enter, and marketing shifts from awareness to differentiation. The product gets refined using customer feedback.
Maturity: sales level off, the market saturates, and competition on price and features intensifies. Decline: sales fall due to competition or obsolescence.
The life cycle guides pricing, promotion, expansion and cost decisions, and products move through the stages at different speeds.
w1d3r2: Full cycle: R&D (costly, no sales, negative cash flow) → introduction → growth → maturity → decline.
Introduction: heavy promotion and negative cash flow. Penetration pricing or price skimming attracts early adopters.
Growth: sales rise fast, competitors appear, and cash flow usually turns positive. Maturity: demand stagnates but costs fall, so cash flow stays positive.
Decline: oversupply, new technology and changing tastes push sales down, ending in clearance pricing and discontinuation.

Extension strategies delay decline. Coca-Cola used line extensions (Diet Coke, Coke Zero, Cherry Coke, the short-lived Coca-Cola Life) and brand extensions. Apple keeps the iPhone growing with regular new models.
w4d1r1: A former Google PM's 6-step structure for answering any PM interview question.

1) Listen actively and take notes on keywords, showing enthusiasm. 2) Ask clarifying questions (users, platforms, domestic vs international), or restate the question: 'You're asking me to... correct?'
3) Pause for 10–15 seconds to think. Interviewers prefer a coherent answer to an instant one.
4) Lay out your structure before diving in (e.g. 'I'll cover three options and their trade-offs'), ideally on a whiteboard, so the interviewer can redirect you.
5) Explain your reasoning confidently with visuals. 6) Check in and pivot if the interviewer's cues suggest you're off track.
w4d4r1: 'What's your favorite product and why?' is one of the most common PM interview questions, so prepare it in advance.
Passion: pick something you genuinely use and care about, not a product chosen to impress. Fake enthusiasm is obvious.
Perspective: have an arguable, nuanced thesis. 'Gmail organizes my email' is bland; take a position someone could disagree with.
Personality: let your interests and product taste show. It builds rapport and shows what you love about product work.
w4d4r2: Framework example: Too Good To Go, an app selling restaurants' surplus food at steep discounts in 'surprise bags'.
Start with why you love it: the mission (tackling food waste) plus the user experience.
Walk through the user journey: search restaurants with filters (nearby, pickup time) → view the profile and ratings → claim a surprise bag → pick up.
Explain value for each side: consumers get affordable food from good restaurants, restaurants recover revenue from waste, and the company likely earns platform fees.
Then identify pain points (e.g. uncertainty about what's in the bag) and propose improvements that fit the product's goals.
w4d4r3: Product improvement questions come as 'favorite product + improve it' or a standalone 'How would you improve X?'

Step 1: name the product and three reasons you love it. Example: Kindle covers the whole reading journey (discovery → reading with notes and dictionary → recommendations), it's easy for all ages, and it has no distractions.
Step 2: define the goal and choose a user segment (e.g. avid fiction readers who follow specific authors).
Step 3: list that segment's pain points, then brainstorm solutions such as book summaries, author fan clubs and Kindle-exclusive short stories.
Step 4: prioritize by impact (how critical the pain point is) vs effort, and pick 1–2 solutions (here: book summaries and author following).
w4d4r4: Mock: 'Design a new feature to improve Google Maps.' The candidate chooses engagement as the goal and mobile as the platform.
Segment users (commuters, travelers, local explorers, businesses), brainstorm each segment's pain points, and pick the most promising segment.
Focus on travelers planning trips, who juggle many apps and tabs.
Solution: a 'Trips' tab next to Explore as a one-stop trip planner covering high-level details (dates, destination), specific activities (hiking, food) and logistics.
Prioritize features, define success metrics tied to engagement, and discuss trade-offs and risks.
w4d4r5: Mock: 'How would you improve Headspace?' A product sense question run by a Coinbase (ex-YouTube) PM.
Clarify: act as a Headspace PM and pick a goal. Engagement, measured as minutes meditated, is chosen as the key metric.
Identify user personas (tech professionals, teachers, students, etc.), choose one segment, and list their pain points.
Brainstorm and prioritize solutions, with the final idea centred on getting users to an early meditation habit.
The interviewer notes it matches real data: Calm found (via Amplitude) that early meditation milestones drive the 'aha moment' and retention.
w2d1n1: Eric Migicovsky (YC partner, Pebble founder): founders must talk to users themselves, at every stage. It can't be handed off to a go-between, and engineers don't get a pass.
Three traps from The Mom Test: pitching your idea, asking about hypotheticals ('would you use this?'), and talking more than you listen. Ask about the person's real past instead.
Five useful questions: what's the hardest part of doing X, tell me about the last time it happened, why was it hard, what have you tried to fix it, and what don't you like about those fixes.
If people haven't already tried to solve the problem, it may not hurt enough. Their current workarounds also show you who you'll really compete with.

To pick a first customer, compare how much the problem costs them, how often it happens and whether they have budget. Later, track the share of users who'd be 'very disappointed' without you (40%+ suggests fit).
w2d1n2: Michael Lynch's review of Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test: people (like your mum) will say polite, encouraging things about your idea, so asking for their opinion tells you little.
Three rules: talk about their life rather than your idea, ask about specific things that already happened rather than the future, and listen far more than you speak.
Compliments, vague claims ('I usually…') and promises ('I'd definitely buy that') are weak data. Steer back to a concrete recent example of the problem.
When someone asks for a feature, dig for the reason behind it. The underlying need often points to a simpler or different solution than the request itself.
A good conversation ends with commitment (their time, reputation or money) and a clear next step. A polite 'keep me posted' is not progress.
w2d1n3: A user interview is a one-on-one research conversation where you ask questions, listen and follow up, to learn about people's experiences, needs and motivations.
Interviews are best for discovery and building empathy. They tell you what people think and do, but they don't test whether a design works; that is what usability tests are for.
Start with clear research goals, then write a short guide of open-ended questions, such as asking about the last time someone did the task. Try it out on a colleague before the real sessions.
Build rapport with easy opening questions, slow down, avoid interrupting, and use neutral prompts like 'tell me more' to get beneath the first answer.
People misremember and say what sounds good, so watch out for leading questions and back interviews up with observation or analytics.
w1d4r1: A user persona is a semi-fictional profile of a target user built from real research. Without one, teams end up designing for 'everyone', which means no one.
Step 1: research. Interview 10–20 users, run surveys and focus groups, and analyze reviews and forums. With no users yet, use market research.
Step 2: group users with similar needs and behaviors into a few distinct segments, one persona each.
Step 3: write the persona's background, goals, daily habits and frustrations (e.g. 'Design Lead Priya, 34, juggles reviews across projects, hates duplicate work').
Steps 4–5: bring it to life with a name, face and setting, share it with the team, and update it as you learn more.
w2d2n1: Clay Christensen tells the milkshake story: a fast-food chain improved its shakes based on what its 'typical milkshake customer' said they wanted, and sales didn't move.
Instead, a researcher watched who bought shakes and when. About half were sold early in the morning to people alone, buying only a shake and driving off.

Asked what 'job' they hired the shake for, commuters said it kept a long, boring drive interesting and kept them full until mid-morning. Bananas, bagels, doughnuts and chocolate bars were the alternatives they'd tried.
So the real competition was other breakfast-on-the-go options, not other milkshakes, and the market was far bigger than the product category suggested.
Lesson: understand the job a customer is trying to get done, in its real situation, before deciding how to improve a product.
w2d2n2: This HBS Working Knowledge piece explains Christensen's view that many new products fail because markets are split by product type or demographics, not by what customers are trying to do.
Demographics may line up with purchases, but they don't cause them. People buy because a job comes up in their lives and they 'hire' a product to do it.

In the milkshake study, morning buyers wanted a filling, slow-to-finish companion for the commute, while after-school buyers were parents treating their kids: two different jobs needing two different shakes.
Brands that name a clear job (Christensen points to FedEx and IKEA) are hard to copy, because a competitor would need to do the whole job better, not just match a feature.
Most company data and store layouts are organised by product or customer type, which makes it hard to see jobs. Managers have to go and look on purpose.
w1d4r3: A user flow maps every step a user takes through your product to complete one specific task, from entry point to goal.
Start from the user's goal and context, and limit each flow to a single task so it stays readable.
Use consistent notation: circles for start and end, rectangles for screens or steps, diamonds for decisions, and arrows for movement in one main direction.
Include error states and alternative paths (wrong password, going back), not just the happy path.
Keep flows simple, share them with designers and engineers, and test them against how real users behave.
w1d4r4: User flows show all the steps a user can take to complete a task, so designers can predict the path and fix problems early.
Notation: circles for start and end, rectangles for steps, diamonds for key decisions, solid lines for the preferred (forward) action, dotted lines for alternatives (like going back).
Login example: has an account? → enter email and password → do they match? → yes: into the app; no: 'forgot password?' → retry, or go to a separate password-recovery flow.
Separate sub-flows (registration, password recovery) are shown as their own circles.
w1d4r5: A user flow diagram shows the path a user takes to reach a goal. It tells you which pages to design and improves your information architecture.
Five elements: start point (an app home, or any landing page for websites), end point, pages/screens, decision points (diamonds) and arrows.
Always make flows contextual: define upfront what the user wants to achieve (e.g. sign in to check bonus points).
Walkthrough in FigJam: home → sign in → enter credentials → valid? → new device? → extra security check. Invalid → error → retry or reset the password by email link.
Tip: solid lines for the primary path and dashed lines for alternatives keep the diagram readable.
w1d4r6: A user journey visualizes the steps a user takes to reach a goal on a timeline, enriched with their thoughts and emotions.
Zomato example: hungry → open app → overwhelmed by options → pick a cuisine → confused between restaurants → choose a dish → pay (happy if there's an offer) → wait for delivery.
Plotting emotions at each step reveals pain points, here the confusion and overload when choosing what and where to order.
The PM's job is to spot these pain points in the journey and design solutions that make that moment easier.
w1d4r9: A journey map shows the process a person goes through to reach a goal: a timeline of their actions, layered with what they think and feel along the way.

Most maps share five parts: an actor (usually a persona), a scenario with the user's goal and expectations, the phases of the journey, the user's actions, thoughts and emotions in each phase, and the opportunities these reveal.
Stick to one actor per map. Different kinds of users take different journeys and need maps of their own.
Journey maps work best for experiences that unfold over time or across several channels, such as shopping online or planning a trip.
The value is twofold: making the map gets the whole team to a shared view of the user, and the finished map is a memorable way to share insights and guide decisions.
w1d4r7: A user flow covers the specific, step-by-step actions to complete one task (e.g. login with error paths), usually drawn as a flowchart.
A user journey map covers the overall experience across touchpoints and phases (e.g. discover → research → buy → support for a laptop), including pain points and opportunities.
Journey maps are high-level, cross-platform and experience/emotion-focused. User flows are detailed, interface-centric and action-focused.
Both focus on the user's goals and pain points and work as communication tools for stakeholders, designers and developers.
w2d4n1: Intercom's rule is 'start with the problem': write a clear problem statement before discussing solutions, so the team designs, judges and scopes ideas against the same goal.
A problem statement is not a spec. It describes what customers need, not what the team has already decided to build.
A good one covers three things: the outcome the customer wants, why they want it, and what is painful about how they do it today.
Example: customers kept asking for 'tickets'. The real need was making sure queries didn't get lost between teams, so Intercom built workflow and automation tools instead of copying ticket numbers.
Understanding the motivation and pain points gives the team clear criteria for comparing solutions, and often leads to a more original product than building the requested feature.
w2d4n2: Competitive analysis helps PMs see the market clearly, spot gaps and decide what to build. Skipping it risks weak positioning and wasted effort.
Think like the user: your competitors are whatever people use instead, including spreadsheets, manual work or doing nothing, not just the brands you'd name.
Start with a reason and a scope (a launch, rising churn, entering a new market), then pick about 5 to 7 main competitors using interviews, support tickets, review sites and sales feedback.

Choose a format that fits the goal: a feature comparison table, SWOT, a positioning map or a jobs-to-be-done comparison. Gather evidence from pricing pages, free trials, reviews, job posts and help docs.
Pay attention to how users feel about each product, not just features. Turn findings into short summaries that feed the roadmap and messaging, and refresh them every quarter or so.
w2d3r2: SWOT analysis assesses Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats. It works for a company, product line, department or even an individual.
Strengths and weaknesses are internal (brand, loyal customers, technology, debt, supply chain). Opportunities and threats are external (new markets, regulation, competitors, economic shifts).
Examples: a tariff cut is an opportunity for a carmaker to export; a drought is a threat to a wheat producer.
It should be realistic, fact-based and data-driven, using input from diverse groups across the organization rather than marketing spin.
Use it to guide strategy toward plans more likely to succeed. Its limitation is that it's a snapshot, not a full plan.
w2d3r3: Porter's Five Forces helps PMs look beyond direct competitors to the full set of pressures that shape a market's profitability.
1) Rivalry among existing competitors. 2) Threat of substitutes, meaning different products that solve the same need.
3) Bargaining power of buyers, which sets their willingness to pay. 4) Bargaining power of suppliers, which sets input costs.
5) Threat of new entrants who could take share, depending on barriers to entry.
PMs use it to step out of daily execution, judge how attractive a market is, and shape strategy and pricing (airlines are a classic example of a market squeezed on every side).
w4d5r2: Meta mock: 'Design a fitness app for Meta.' Start by asking why Meta wants it: to get the community off screens and active together in the real world.
Set a mission-aligned goal ('bring the world together through activity and fitness') with sub-goals measured by acquisition and engagement.
Use Meta's huge user base for market segmentation, then pick a target segment whose needs fit the goal.
Identify that segment's pain points, brainstorm solutions, and prioritize, keeping a clear line from mission → goal → segment → solution.
Address safety and resources (healthy, safe programs at scale) and get to pain points and solutions quickly.
w4d5r3: Exponent mock interview: 'Design a refrigerator for kids,' answered by Diego Granados (Microsoft AI/ML PM), who explains his reasoning as he goes.
Common mistake: rushing to solutions. He first asks clarifying questions: what type of company (assume a connected-appliance company with data, AI and cloud) and what constraints.
Pain points: kids can't tell what's inside the fridge (containers, raw food), so they go for the easy option. Parents worry about unhealthy choices even when healthy food is available.
He proposes three solutions (including a game-like system), checks them against a parent's concerns, prioritizes them, and defines success through sales, returns and support calls.
Interviewer tip: lay your structure out visually (numbered, spatially) so the interviewer can follow your thinking.
w3d1n1: Marty Cagan (SVPG): empowered teams can only make good decisions if they understand the bigger picture, which comes from a product vision and a product strategy.
The product vision describes the future you're trying to create, usually 2 to 5 years out (longer for hardware). It should inspire people, more like a story or prototype than a spec.
A strong vision also helps recruit great people. Leaders should be stubborn on the vision but flexible on the details.
Product strategy is the plan for getting from today to that vision. It decides which problems to solve, while discovery finds solutions and delivery builds them.

Good strategy means making hard choices about focus, generating insights, turning insights into action, and actively managing without micromanaging. Many companies have goals and roadmaps but no real strategy.
w3d1n2: Gibson Biddle (former VP of Product at Netflix) explains how his product strategy models fit together around four questions: what are we building long-term, what matters most now, how will we deliver it, and when.
Long-term: positioning and brand describe what the product is and promises. His GLEe model sets the sequence: Get big first, then Lead, then expand.
Priorities: with the GEM model, leaders force-rank Growth, Engagement and Monetization (each with a proxy metric) so everyone agrees on what comes first.
Delivery: the DHM model asks how the product will Delight customers in Hard-to-copy, Margin-enhancing ways. The SMT lockup pairs each Strategy with a Metric and the Tactics that test it.
A company-level strategy sets the frame, while each team (like Netflix's personalization team) writes its own more detailed version. The two are refined together, top-down and bottom-up.
w2d3r7: The Ansoff Matrix plans growth strategy along two axes, existing vs new products and existing vs new markets, giving four strategies.
Market penetration (existing product, existing market): sell more through marketing, promotions and pricing, e.g. McDonald's pushing Big Mac sales. Lowest risk.
Product development (new product, existing market): innovate for current customers, e.g. McDonald's launching the McPlant in the UK. Being first to market matters.
Market development (existing product, new market): take products to new regions or segments.
Diversification (new product, new market): highest risk, but can open entirely new revenue streams.
w3d2n1: Sean McBride (Intercom): prioritization is hard because people favour pet ideas, clever ideas and new ideas, and they underestimate effort. RICE makes the comparison more consistent.
Reach: how many people the project affects in a set period (e.g. customers per quarter), using real product data where possible.

Impact: how much it moves the goal for each person, on a scale of 3 (massive), 2 (high), 1 (medium), 0.5 (low) and 0.25 (minimal). Confidence: 100%, 80% or 50%, depending on how solid the estimates are.
Effort: total person-months across product, design and engineering. Score = Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort, i.e. expected impact per unit of work.
Treat the score as a guide, not a rule. Dependencies or must-have work can justify doing a lower-scoring project first, and the score makes that trade-off visible.
w2d4r1: Prioritization frameworks don't produce the answer on their own. They make trade-offs visible and defensible, so the team can debate on shared terms (and answer loud stakeholders).
Quantitative scoring: RICE (Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort, from Intercom) and Value vs Effort are the fastest to start with. They ignore dependencies, and their estimates are subjective.
Customer-input methods: the Kano Model (must-haves vs delighters, via surveys), opportunity scoring (importance vs satisfaction), Product Tree and Buy a Feature (customer workshops and games).
Release scoping: the Story Map (MVP and release slices) and MoSCoW (Must/Should/Could/Won't), where teams tend to overinflate the Must-haves.
Cost of Delay puts a money value on waiting (weekly value ÷ build time). Running two frameworks on the same backlog often reveals hidden bias.
w2d2r2: MVPs are often misunderstood as 'the least amount of work'. A real MVP is the smallest thing you can build to learn something about your product or users.
An MVP can be a landing page, a prototype or a basic working product. Its goals are to learn perceived user value quickly and gather real-world feedback.
Benefits: early feedback from real users, fewer sunk costs if the idea doesn't work, and lean development focused on essentials.
Steps: identify the core audience problem → decide on features and functionality → design a prototype → launch and gather feedback → scale into a more robust product.
Best practice: collect and react to user feedback continuously. Watch out for building too little to learn anything, or too much.
w2d2r3: 42% of startups fail because there's no market need. An MVP tests viability with real users before investing in a full product.
An MVP is the simplest version of a product with just enough features to attract early customers and gather feedback.
Three key elements: enough features for people to want it, a feedback mechanism, and benefits for early adopters.
Famous MVPs: Amazon started selling used college textbooks online; Airbnb started by renting out air mattresses through a simple website.
Plan by focusing on core features only, launching quickly, then iterating based on what users actually want.
w2d2r4: Collection of famous MVPs: Facebook, Groupon, Airbnb, Zynga, Pebble, Amazon, Zappos, Etsy, Dropbox, Buffer, Twitter, Foursquare, Spotify, Uber, the iPhone, AngelList and Product Hunt.

Common patterns: Dropbox validated demand with an explainer video before building, Zappos manually bought shoes from stores to fulfil orders, Buffer used a landing page to test interest, and Product Hunt began as an email list.
Lesson: the first version is often very basic, manual or limited in scope. The goal is to validate demand and learn, not to impress.
Many giants started in one narrow niche (Facebook at Harvard, Amazon with books, Uber with black cars in San Francisco) before expanding.
w3d3r1: A PRD (Product Requirements Document), mainly written by the PM, answers three questions: why build it, what it should do, and how success will be measured. It's a common APM interview topic.
It aligns engineering, design, support and sales on one picture, and balances engineering's functional concerns with design's focus on usability. It should not dictate 'how' to build.

Five tips: describe the problem and leave room for solutions, keep it concise (a few pages), keep it updated (add a 'Recent Updates' log), get stakeholder feedback in the doc, and apply the 'rule of 5' (five random teammates should describe purpose, timeline, status and features the same way).
Writing a PRD forces you to think end to end (dependencies), separate must-haves from nice-to-haves for the MVP, and validate assumptions.
Other docs build on it: engineering tech specs and architecture docs, design wireframes and mockups, and QA test plans.
w1d5r1: A wireframe is a 2D blueprint of a digital product's interface: grayscale, no-frills and clearly not the final design. Its main goal is team alignment before coding starts.
PMs should understand wireframes to speak designers' language, influence without authority, and sketch their own ideas instead of describing them vaguely.

Low fidelity: rough sketches that capture the idea and flow. Mid fidelity: more concrete layouts, still grayscale. High fidelity: pixel-specific, with interactivity, menus, microcopy, images and colors.
Move to the next fidelity only after the previous one is approved, and really listen to feedback.
Tools: pen and paper, Figma (collaborative and cloud-based) and Balsamiq (an industry classic). A wireframe still needs the PM to explain the 'why' behind it.
w1d5r2: Wireframes aren't a visual copy of the product. They communicate what the user should do to get value and whether that matches what the business needs.
Conceptual design: the mental model users expect (e.g. Uber uses a map because transport means moving between two places).
Information structure: the essential inputs users expect (e.g. every flight site asks from, to, date, passengers).
Functional layers: information design and interaction design, meaning what happens when users click, add to cart, and so on.
Worked example: a premium e-commerce app where the homepage is built around the main intent (easy product discovery), with promotions as a secondary intent.
w1d5r3: A wireframe is a basic outline of a digital experience, used to visualize ideas, communicate clearly and iterate fast.
In Figma: create a design file, add a phone-sized frame (the 'paper'), and paste a reference screenshot (e.g. the YouTube app) resized to match.
You only need two tools, rectangles and text. Start with the biggest element (the thumbnail), then add the timestamp, avatar (ellipse, with Shift for a perfect circle), title and icons.
Write real copy instead of Lorem Ipsum to catch overlooked details. Shortcuts: R = rectangle, T = text, L = line, O = ellipse.
Stick to grayscale so attention stays on layout and structure.
w1d5r4: Wireframe: a low-fidelity, grayscale blueprint of layout and structure (what goes where). Quick and cheap to change.
Mockup: a static, high-fidelity visual design with real colors, typography, images and branding, showing how the product will look.
Prototype: an interactive simulation of the product that you can click through, used to test flows and usability with users before building.
They usually progress in that order, adding fidelity and cost at each step, so settle structure early and polish later.
w3d1r1: A Google PM (Liam Bolling) explains how deep a PM needs to go: a PM sits between UX, business and engineering, and needs to know each category well without being an expert in any.

Tech basics: how the internet works at a high level, how data is stored (data types like integer, double and string), what an API is and why it needs a key, what programming languages are used for, web vs native apps, and what servers and latency are.

Be able to break problems into smaller high-level solutions with engineers, own your metrics (it's never just 'daily active users') and draw the architecture diagram of boxes and arrows with confidence.

SQL is the one technical skill worth learning so you can pull your own data. Avoid buzzwords like AI, blockchain or ML unless you know what they mean. Don't have opinions on specific technologies. You've gone too far if you're the best engineer on the team.

Business skills: revenue, costs, profit and EBITDA, pricing and monetization models (freemium, ad-supported, pay once, subscription), and understanding why competitors succeed or fail. Learn from free courses and tech news.
w3d1r2: An API (application programming interface) lets two systems communicate: system A sends a request, system B does the work and sends back a response. A big part of a PM's job is talking to engineers, so this is a core concept.
Restaurant analogy: the waiter takes your order from a menu, passes it to the kitchen and brings back the food. The menu defines what you can ask for and how.
Movie-ticket app example: giving your location as a parameter makes an API fetch the movies playing in your city. Searching for a movie triggers another API call.
Endpoints are the different addresses of an API (like different doors of a house), e.g. the Google Maps text search endpoint, which returns places for a query such as 'pizza in New York'.
Responses come back as JSON (e.g. address, photos, ratings). Also covered: parameters, payloads, and GET (fetch data) versus POST (send data) requests.
w3d1r3: A database is an organized collection of information stored electronically. It can be structured (tables of rows and columns, like a spreadsheet) or unstructured.
E-commerce example: a Customers table (customer ID, name, address, phone) and an Orders table (order ID, customer ID, item count, total cost) together form a database.
Relational (SQL) databases store data in related tables. Non-relational (NoSQL) databases store data more flexibly. Which to choose depends on the use case.
Primary key: a unique identifier for each record (e.g. customer ID), essential for retrieving or updating the right row when two customers share a name.
Foreign key: a column that links two tables (e.g. customer ID in Orders), so you can fetch all orders for a given customer.
w3d2r3: A server is a computer that provides services (websites, data, email, files) to client machines over the internet or a local network.
'Server' is a role, not a type of hardware. Any desktop can act as a file or web server, but desktops can't handle heavy loads or many simultaneous connections.
Large organizations dedicate servers to one service each (web, database, email). Small ones may run several services on one machine.
Real servers run 24/7 and use specialized, redundant hardware (multiple drives, power supplies, ECC memory) and server operating systems built for many concurrent connections.
Common types: web, file, database, email, DNS and application servers.
w3d2r2: The SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) is the structured process for building software from client requirements. Example: Adam's online home-decor store.
1) Planning: agree the app's purpose, end users and key elements. 2) Requirement analysis: detail each element, security and risks, and document them in an SRS (Software Requirements Specification).
3) Design: architects create the system design from the SRS, recorded in a DDS (Design Document Specification).
4) Implementation: developers write the code. 5) Testing: QA finds and fixes bugs and checks requirements are met.
6) Deployment and maintenance: release to users, then fix issues and add updates over time. Models like Waterfall and Agile run these phases differently.
w2d4r4: Waterfall: a linear, sequential process (requirements → design → build → test → deploy) where each phase finishes before the next begins and changes later are costly.
Agile: work in short iterative cycles (sprints), delivering small working pieces, gathering customer feedback each cycle and adapting.
Agile benefits: transparency for clients, who see progress and give feedback every sprint, more predictable cost and schedule per sprint, and easy change.
Waterfall suits projects with fixed, well-understood requirements and strict documentation needs. Agile suits evolving requirements and fast-changing markets.
Most modern software and product teams use Agile (Scrum, Kanban) because requirements rarely stay fixed.
w2d4r6: Both Scrum and Kanban are Agile pull systems. The Product Owner keeps a prioritized Product Backlog of features and user stories, and value ships in small increments with feedback.

Scrum: fixed sprints (usually 2 weeks). Sprint Planning pulls items into a Sprint Backlog, new work waits until the next sprint, there's a daily 15-minute stand-up, and each sprint ends with a Sprint Review (demo) and Retrospective.
Kanban: a continuous flow with no sprints or sprint backlog. The pull happens through Work-in-Progress (WIP) limits on each board column, and an empty slot signals the team to pull the next item.
Roles: Scrum Master (Scrum) or Agile Coach (Kanban) helps the team keep good habits. Kanban teams also often hold stand-ups, demos and retros.
Neither is as rigid as it sounds. High-performing teams adapt the system to what works for them.
w4d1r2: Kevin Way (Amazon senior PM) on 'Should company X get into space Y?' questions, which test business goals, market risks and opportunities, and internal and external factors.
Structure: clarify the company's goals (what it does, how it makes money, current focus) → analyze what helps or hinders it → pick the factors that matter most → make a recommendation.
Frameworks to choose from (none is wrong): the 5Cs (Customers, Company, Collaborators, Competitors, Climate), SWOT, or Porter's Five Forces. Just cover both internal and external considerations.
Worked example, 'Should Google build a modular phone?': first-mover advantage but unproven and costly, and a key tension is ecosystem vs revenue (more Android users vs less revenue per device).
Say what you plan to jot down, tee up the central trade-off, then end with a confident recommendation tied to the company's goal. It doesn't need to be all-or-nothing.
w4d1r3: Strategy and GTM questions usually take the form 'Should X enter market Y?' (e.g. Google into streaming, Facebook into dating, Swiggy/Zomato into restaurants). They test executive-level, structured thinking.
Don't jump to yes or no. Clarify the company's goals and motivation first, then work through a structured process.

5C framework: Competition (how crowded, any unfair advantages?), Customers (synergy between current and new customers; Facebook → dating makes sense, Facebook → cloud doesn't), Company (capabilities, assets, fit).
Collaborators: which partners you'd need. Climate: regulatory, political and economic environment, licences, purchasing power.
Weigh the evidence from each C, make a clear go or no-go call, then outline how to enter (build, partner or acquire) and the risks.
w4d1r4: Google mock: 'You're the new CEO of Uber. What's your 10-year strategy?' Stay high-level and focus on the big bets.
Clarify the context (profitability struggles, intense competition), then set a mission: 'Be the way you move', covering both people and things.
Define consumer tenets to guide decisions: fast and convenient, safe, environmentally conscious.
Build strategic pillars from strengths such as network effects and global distribution, with expansion into local markets through competition or acquisition, which needs a strong capital base.
Strong answers articulate a vision, stress-test their own plan ('throw darts at my own solution') and tie every pillar back to the mission.
w2d5r1: A go-to-market (GTM) strategy turns a product bet into measurable market outcomes. It's a cross-functional plan, not just a launch checklist.
It answers four questions: who are we targeting and why, what problem we solve and why we're the best solution, how we'll reach, convert and support customers, and how we'll know it's working.
GTM connects company strategy with day-to-day execution, aligning product, product marketing, sales and customer success around one value proposition and narrative.
Lisa Kamm (Dow Jones): judge launches on outcomes, not outputs. Ask 'did it create the expected outcome?' rather than 'did we launch?'
A good GTM makes ownership explicit and sets the metrics that tell you when to change course.
w2d5r2: GTM strategy answers three questions: where to play, what to sell, and how to engage.
Layer 1, target market and ideal customer profile (ICP): by vertical, company size or geography.
Layer 2, unique value proposition per persona: messaging that resonates rationally and emotionally and creates urgency.
Layer 3, route to market: inside sales, e-commerce, direct sales reps or partners. Layer 4, packaging and pricing: free trials, freemium, land-and-expand, good-better-best tiers.
Layer 5, tactics: brand awareness → lead generation → sales enablement and training.
w2d5r3: An investor's view (Steve Barsh of Dreamit Ventures, on Slidebean) of the go-to-market slide in a pitch deck. Investors want to see an efficient, focused plan to win early customers with the fewest resources.
'We'll do direct sales' or 'online sales' is not a GTM strategy. Those are sales tactics.

Fishing analogy: fish where the fish are. Going offshore for tuna (big enterprise deals) means 12–18 month sales cycles that can outlast your runway. Fish in the bay instead: closer, easier, quicker catches.

Choose targeting criteria such as a searing pain point, a buyer who is the decision maker (faster closes), geographic closeness for feedback, and a price point that fits their typical budgets. 'Push sand down a hill, not up.'
This first segment is your beachhead. Repeat the process to rank follow-on markets, and remember that tactics are wasted if the underlying strategy isn't tuned.
w2d5r4: A SaaS founder's three GTM channel principles for driving growth, mapped to how aware buyers are.

Principle 1: win the roughly 3% of your ICP who already know their problem and are choosing a solution. The main channel is Google search ads on high-intent keywords (e.g. 'referral marketing platform').
Principle 2: get in front of ideal customers who aren't actively buying yet and educate them with content that builds awareness and trust before they're in market.
Principle 3: proactive outbound with very simple, direct messages to target accounts.
Matching channels to the buyer's stage (aware and searching vs unaware) lets you capture demand now while building future pipeline.
w2d5r5: A GTM strategy is the plan to bring your product to target customers through the right channels. It comes after positioning and messaging.
Pre-launch: build awareness and credibility by educating your target market, growing an organic following that beta tests and spreads the word.
Launch: drive adoption by announcing across all organic channels and amplifying with paid ads.
Post-launch: optimize and scale. Cut channels that don't work, double down on those that do, and test new ones.
Template per phase: objective, KPI (SMART), timeline, plus a table of channels, activities and resources. Worked example: a reading app for children with learning disabilities.
w2d5r6: Ten common pricing strategies: competition-based, cost-plus, freemium, dynamic, skimming, penetration, economy, premium, bundle and psychological.
Competition-based: benchmark against rivals (Pepsi vs Coca-Cola). Common in saturated markets, but ignores your costs and demand.
Cost-plus: cost plus a fixed markup. Simple, but ignores customer value and competitors and weakens the incentive to cut costs.
Skimming (start high, then lower, e.g. new tech) vs penetration (start low to win share fast). Dynamic pricing changes with demand (airlines, ride-hailing).
Freemium (free base, paid upgrades), premium (price signals quality), economy (low cost, high volume), bundles (packages that raise order value) and psychological pricing (e.g. $9.99).
w2d5r7: Charm pricing: $1.99 feels like $1 because our brains anchor on the first digit, which is especially strong just below 10, 100 or 1,000.
Premium or exclusive pricing: brands like Apple and luxury labels sell status and lifestyle, not specs, so a higher price adds appeal.
Visual tricks: small fonts and no commas ($2399 vs $2,399) make prices feel smaller, and words that suggest 'small' soften big prices.
Price partitioning: '$3 a day' sounds cheaper than a monthly fee, even though per-visit cost is often far higher.
Precise prices ($29,654.37) feel honest and invite less haggling. Round prices work better for emotional purchases like wedding rings.
w2d1r1: Revenue alone is a poor guide to product success. Every product needs its own north star that reflects the value it delivers.
Context matters: Hinge is 'designed to be deleted', so users leaving after finding a partner is 'good churn', a success metric rather than a failure.
Metrics give an aggregated view of how users behave (e.g. Bumble saw a 56% spike in video calls early in the 2020 lockdowns and doubled down on virtual dating).

Pick metrics from your goals. The three fundamentals are acquiring users, retaining them, and growing revenue, each with its own metrics (traffic, sources and acquisition cost; engagement and retention; revenue).
Products must eventually make money and keep costs low. Vine was culturally huge but shut down in 2017 for lack of monetization.
w2d1r3: A metric is any measurement of size or scale (e.g. your weight on a scale), tracked over time.
A KPI is a metric tied directly to a stated goal or objective with a target and timeframe (e.g. lose 35 lb in 7 months for a reunion = 5 lb per month).
Every KPI is a metric, but not every metric is a KPI. What makes the difference is intent and a strategy to control and improve the number.
KPIs drive action: if you're off target (lost only 4 lb in month two), you adjust the plan (6 lb next month) to get back on track.
w4d2n1: Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson and Xin Fu (Google, 2010) introduce HEART, a framework for user-centred metrics, as a complement to common business and technical metrics.
Common 'PULSE' metrics (Page views, Uptime, Latency, Seven-day active users, Earnings) matter, but they're indirect. More page views could mean a feature is popular, or that users are lost.

HEART categories: Happiness (satisfaction surveys), Engagement (e.g. share of users active 5+ days a week in Gmail), Adoption (new users), Retention (users who come back), and Task success (completion, time, errors).
Not every category fits every product. Use the framework to decide on purpose which ones to include, for the whole product or for a single feature.

Goals, Signals, Metrics: agree on the goal first, then the user behaviour or attitude that would show success, then a metric to track. Prefer averages and ratios over raw counts that grow with the user base.
w2d1r2: HEART (Google) measures user experience quality: Happiness (satisfaction, NPS), Engagement (usage depth and frequency), Adoption (new users or feature uptake), Retention (users who come back) and Task success (completion rate, errors, time on task).
Apply HEART with Goals → Signals → Metrics: define the goal for each dimension, the user behavior that signals it, then the metric that measures it.
AARRR ('pirate metrics', Dave McClure) tracks the customer lifecycle funnel: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue.
Use AARRR to find where the funnel leaks (e.g. many signups but poor activation) and HEART to judge the quality of the experience. The two complement each other.
w4d2n2: Amplitude: a North Star Metric is the one measure that best captures the value customers get from your product, and links that value to future revenue.
It helps teams agree on what to improve, show the impact of their work and hold themselves accountable for outcomes rather than output.
A good North Star reflects real customer value and is a leading indicator. Monthly revenue is a lagging result, and raw daily active users can be a vanity number.
Pair one North Star with 3 to 5 input metrics the team can actually move, looking at breadth, depth, frequency and efficiency of use.
Most products play one of three 'games': attention, transactions or productivity. Knowing yours helps pick the metric. An early Facebook example: users who added 7 friends within 10 days.
w2d1r5: Many teams have great dashboards, perfect north star metrics and product-led growth frameworks, and still fail. Metrics alone aren't the problem.
At Stripe, Patrick Collison asked a pivotal question in a product review: 'Have you talked to customers who signed up but then didn't engage?'
The most overlooked signal: users who showed real intent (signed up and maybe took a few core actions) and then dropped off.
Define an intent threshold for your product (e.g. created a base, filled it and shared it in Airtable), then talk to the people who crossed it but didn't stick, to learn what blocked them.
Understanding these high-intent drop-offs is what unlocks early-stage product-led growth, more than any metric framework.
w4d3n1: Product Space: an A/B test randomly shows users a control (A) or a variant (B) and measures which performs better, replacing gut feel with evidence and limiting risk.

Good candidates: button placement, onboarding copy, email subject lines, pricing and trial setups, and ranking or recommendation changes. Skip it for low-traffic features, big redesigns or urgent decisions.
Plan first: define the problem, write a testable hypothesis with an expected result, and choose a primary metric plus secondary and 'guardrail' metrics that must not get worse.
Work out the sample size you need before starting, split traffic evenly, run the test across full weekly cycles, and check that the groups really are the expected sizes.
Judge results on statistical significance (often 95%), effect size and confidence intervals. Common mistakes are stopping early as soon as the result looks good and testing too many things at once.
w2d2r6: PMF is when your product strongly matches market demand and users become enthusiastic advocates, driving organic growth.
Know your customer: their challenges, current alternatives and pain points, through research and interviews.
Craft a clear value proposition that answers 'Why choose us over the competition?', focused on the problem you uniquely solve.
Build an MVP for early adopters and iterate in build–test–learn–refine cycles based on their feedback.
Signs of PMF: high engagement, low churn, and rising referrals and word of mouth. It isn't a one-time milestone, because markets and competitors keep changing.
w4d3n2: Rahul Vohra (Superhuman CEO) wanted a way to measure product-market fit before launch, because common definitions only tell you once you have it.
He used Sean Ellis's question, 'How would you feel if you could no longer use the product?' If 40% or more say 'very disappointed', you likely have fit. Superhuman started at 22%.
Step 1: describe the users who'd be very disappointed and focus on people like them. Just narrowing to that segment raised the score to 33%.
Step 2: ignore users who wouldn't care, and study the 'somewhat disappointed' ones who love the main benefit (speed). Find what holds them back, e.g. no mobile app.
Step 3: spend half the roadmap on what fans love and half on fixing what blocks the near-fans, then re-survey regularly. The score reached 58% within three quarters.
w2d2r7: Product-market fit simply asks whether your product is needed and whether people are eager to pay for it, with a clear USP versus competitors.
Warning signs of no PMF: low customer response, negative or no press, and high visibility with no engagement.
Amazon Fire Phone (2014): overpriced, locked into Amazon's ecosystem, and its 3D gimmick didn't solve a real need. It lost about $170M.

New Coke (1985): nobody had asked for a new recipe to replace a beloved product, and the backlash forced a reversal. Microsoft Zune (2006): arrived after the iPod already owned the market, with no compelling reason to switch.
The road to PMF runs through an MVP: test and learn before committing heavily.
w3d1r5: Bro Code's SQL Full Course, Part 1 (0:00–33:32): install MySQL and MySQL Workbench on Windows or macOS.
Databases: CREATE DATABASE, USE, DROP DATABASE, and setting a database to read-only.
Tables: CREATE TABLE with column names and data types (INT, VARCHAR, DECIMAL, DATE), plus RENAME, ALTER TABLE ADD/MODIFY/DROP COLUMN.
INSERT INTO ... VALUES to add single or multiple rows, including inserting only selected columns.
SELECT to read data: SELECT * vs specific columns, and filtering with WHERE (=, !=, >, <, IS NULL).
w3d1r6: LeetCode's Top SQL 50 study plan, problems 1–10: the Select section (Recyclable and Low Fat Products, Find Customer Referee, Big Countries, Article Views I, Invalid Tweets) and the first Basic Joins problems.
Skills practised: SELECT with WHERE filters, AND/OR conditions, handling NULLs (e.g. referee_id IS NULL OR referee_id != 2), DISTINCT and string length checks.

Joins introduced: LEFT JOIN to keep unmatched rows (Replace Employee ID, Customers Who Visited but Did Not Make Transactions), INNER JOIN for matched data, and self-joins on dates (Rising Temperature).
Tip: write the query yourself first, then compare with the Editorial and community solutions to learn cleaner patterns.
w4d3r1: Guesstimates test your approach, not the final number: break an estimate into logical, calculable pieces. They're common in consulting and non-tech interviews.
There's rarely one right way. Most guesstimates can be solved several ways.
Demand-side approach: start from population and segment down by who uses or buys the thing and how often.
Supply-side approach: start from a constraint such as capacity, area or resources (e.g. outlets × capacity × utilization).
Interviewers may ask for a second approach, so solving it both ways earns extra credit. State your assumptions clearly and sanity-check the result.
w4d3r10: XLRI CRUX club's quick-reference cheat sheet of standard numbers and assumptions for solving guesstimates.
Covers general cases (population, households, demographic splits, urban/rural ratios and similar figures) so you can start estimates confidently.
Includes a separate cheat sheet for policy-related cases (Samagra-style public policy questions).
Use it to memorize a few anchor figures, but always state your assumptions out loud in interviews.
w4d3r3: Real ISB placement guesstimate: how many kites are sold (and flown) during Makar Sankranti?
Break it into kites per person × number of people flying kites during the festival.
Kites per person: assume about 2 days of flying and about 8 hours a day after sleep and other activities, with kites getting cut regularly, so people use several each.
Number of kite flyers: start from the relevant population (states that celebrate), then narrow by age group and participation rates.
Key lesson: the exact answer matters less than a clear, step-by-step breakdown with stated assumptions.
w4d3r5: Type 1 guesstimates are market sizing. Worked example: how many electric vehicles will be sold in India in 2021?
Try it yourself first, then compare. A different approach isn't wrong if it's logical.
Follow a structure: clarify scope (which vehicles: two-wheelers, cars, three-wheelers?), choose demand or supply side, then segment.
Segment by vehicle type and buyer group, apply adoption rates for EVs within total vehicle sales, then add it up.
Close with a sanity check and note the key assumptions driving the number.
w4d3r6: MBB-style supply-side guesstimate: how many flights fly out of Delhi in a day?
Clarify first: only IGI airport, or also military (Hindon) and other airports? What kind of day (weekday or weekend, season)? Assume an average day.
Don't start from population. This is a capacity problem, so use the supply side: runways, operating hours and the take-off rate per runway.
Flights = runways × operational hours × departures per runway per hour × utilization, adjusted for peak vs off-peak hours.
Sanity-check against known benchmarks (busy hub airports handle hundreds of departures a day).
w4d4n2: A tech-style guesstimate: estimate how much storage Google Maps needs.
Start by defining the problem and agreeing on scope before doing any maths.
Write a high-level equation that splits total storage into parts you can estimate one at a time.
Estimate each part in turn: street names, then location (place) names, then logos and images.
The approach shown is one way to solve it. Other breakdowns are valid, as long as they are structured and the assumptions are stated.
w4d2r1: Root cause analysis (RCA) questions give you a metric change (e.g. Facebook Groups creation down 15%, Slack email open rate down 10%) and ask you to diagnose it.
Interviewers look for three things: understanding the metric in context of the whole product, data-driven hypotheses, and a structured approach.
Step 1: clarify the metric definition and its link to the north star. A drop in DoorDash orders is clearly bad; fewer YouTube videos watched may not be if watch time is up.
Step 2: characterize the change: sudden or gradual, seen before, seasonal? Sudden drops usually aren't behavioral and may be system glitches.

Step 3: rule out data and tracking issues, then segment (platform, region, user type, funnel step) and look at internal changes (releases, campaigns) vs external factors (competitors, news, regulation).
w4d2r3: Mock: Flipkart has seen a 15% decline in add-to-cart over the last 3 days. Diagnose it.
The candidate clarifies the scope and lays out a plan, then checks external factors first: competitor launches or sales, and big events like Big Billion Days.
Narrows it down by segment: location (no impact; the drop is spread everywhere), user segments, platforms and categories.
Walks through the user flow (search → product page → add to cart) to locate where in the funnel the drop happens.
Feedback: keep it conversational, ask questions, and course-correct as you go rather than getting lost in your own framework. Practise mocks with peers.
w4d2r4: RCA mock on Urban Company: app usage dropped by about 6–7%.

Framework, from closest to furthest: 1) your own product (start by validating the analytics tool and data), 2) releases by other teams last week, 3) company-level changes in strategy or marketing messaging.
4) External factors: political changes, industry news, or regional events (e.g. restrictions in some areas) outside the company's control.
Segment by service category, city, platform and user type to localize the drop before forming hypotheses.
Career tip: engineers moving into PM should take on product-thinking projects (why a feature exists, how it's marketed) to build a track record.
w4d5n1: A root cause analysis (RCA) mock interview set on YouTube, from a series on product execution questions.
Begin by defining the problem clearly before looking for causes.
Check external factors first: things outside the product that could explain the change.
Then walk through the user journey and dig into funnel metrics to find where behaviour changed.
Narrow the evidence down to a root cause, and only then propose solutions that address it.
w4d5n2: A Meta-style AI PM mock interview: downvotes on ChatGPT answers have been rising steadily, and the candidate has to work out why.
The candidate works through it in a structured, hypothesis-driven way, the same RCA approach used for any metric change.
Hypotheses include changes in user behaviour and changes in notification strategy.
Product bugs and policy changes are also checked as possible causes.
w5d1r1: AI product management means taking a product whose core value comes from AI/ML from concept to launch and ongoing operation, owning the vision, data strategy and model evaluation process.

Test for an AI product: if you remove the AI and it still works the same, it's not an AI product. Recommendation engines, fraud detection and generative assistants are AI products; a bolted-on chatbot is just an AI feature.

Versus traditional PM: the same core (vision, discovery, MVPs, GTM), plus owning a data strategy, managing behavior that shifts after release, tracking model metrics alongside product metrics, and handling fairness and explainability.

Three types: the AI-powered PM (uses AI tools to work faster), the applied/AI-enabled PM (integrates pre-trained models and LLM APIs into products) and the core/platform AI PM (builds foundation models or ML platforms, needs deep ML knowledge).
AI PMs balance product metrics against model performance, risk and responsible-AI guardrails across an AI-specific lifecycle.
w5d1r3: In 2023 Netflix offered up to $900,000 for an AI product manager, showing how much companies value the role. The fundamentals (solve real customer problems, own the product lifecycle) stay the same, but the process changes.

Lifecycle: traditional features are deterministic, but AI work is data-driven and experimental. Accessing and cleaning data can take months, models are trained and tuned iteratively (frameworks like CRISP-DM), and the work continues after launch as new data arrives.
Timelines are less predictable. AI PMs set progress milestones instead of fixed delivery dates and plan fallbacks in case the ML approach doesn't meet the bar.
Stakeholders widen: data scientists, data engineers and ML engineers daily, plus legal, compliance and privacy teams. The PM also manages executive hype by explaining what the model can and can't do.

Experimentation and evaluation: treat each model version like an A/B test, design fail-safes, and track model metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, AUC) alongside product metrics, accepting trade-offs between accuracy, speed and cost.
w5d1r5: AI vs ML vs LLM: AI is the umbrella (systems that reason and act), ML learns patterns from data without explicit rules, and LLMs (GPT, Claude) are ML models trained on huge text datasets to predict the next token.

Prompt engineering: the same model gives very different output for 'summarize this report' vs 'summarize in 3 bullets for a CEO with 30 seconds'. AI PMs build prompt systems (structured templates), not one-off magic prompts.
AI agents and workflows: systems that decide and take multi-step actions. Fine-tuning: further training a model on your data for a specialized task or style.

RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) lets models pull fresh or private data (docs, wikis, databases) to ground answers. Hallucination is confident but false output. Guardrails and safety constrain what the model can say or do.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is like 'Bluetooth for AI', plugging models into tools such as CRMs and email. Evals measure how well your AI actually performs and are essential before and after launch.
w5d2r2: Non-technical PMs need AI/ML fundamentals to build and manage AI products effectively.
AI is the broad goal of machines performing intelligent tasks. ML is the subset where systems learn from data instead of explicit rules.
Key components: data (collected, cleaned, preprocessed), algorithms (learning procedures), models (the trained result), training, and evaluation on unseen data.
Best practices: define the problem and business objective clearly, manage data quality, choose suitable tools (TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn), and build a multidisciplinary team.
Develop iteratively: start with an MVP, test, gather feedback and improve, and consider ethics and bias throughout.
w5d2r4: An LLM is essentially two files: a huge parameters file (e.g. Llama 2 70B is about 140GB) and a small program that runs it. Pretraining compresses a large chunk of the internet (about 10TB of text, thousands of GPUs, millions of dollars) into those weights.
The core task is next-word prediction, which forces the model to learn a lot about the world. The knowledge is lossy and 'dreamed', which is why models hallucinate.
Base model → assistant: fine-tune on high-quality Q&A conversations written by human labelers, then refine with human feedback (RLHF).

Capabilities scale predictably with model size and data (scaling laws). Modern LLMs use tools (browsing, calculator, code), are multimodal, and are moving toward slower 'System 2' reasoning and self-improvement. Karpathy frames the LLM as the kernel of a new operating system.
Security challenges: jailbreaks, prompt injection (hidden instructions in web pages or images) and data poisoning/backdoors.
w5d2r6: GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer. It generates text by repeatedly predicting a probability distribution over the next token, sampling one, appending it, and repeating.
Text is split into tokens, and each token becomes a vector (embedding). Directions in embedding space encode meaning (e.g. king − man + woman ≈ queen).
Inside a transformer, attention blocks let vectors share context with each other, and MLP blocks process each vector. Repeating these layers refines meaning.
Deep learning premise: all behavior comes from tunable weights (GPT-3 has about 175B) organized in matrices, learned from data rather than hand-coded.
At the end, unembedding turns the final vector into scores for every token, and softmax with temperature converts them into probabilities (higher temperature means more random, creative output).
w3d4r3: Notes on Google's Prompting Essentials course (four modules): prompting fundamentals, everyday work tasks (emails, brainstorming, tables, summaries), data analysis and presentations, and AI as a creative or expert partner.
Five-step framework, 'Tiny Crabs Ride Enormous Iguanas': Task (include a persona and output format), Context, References (examples), Evaluate the output, Iterate.

If results fall short: revisit the framework (more context or examples), split the prompt into shorter sentences, rephrase or switch to an analogous task (e.g. 'write a story' instead of 'a marketing plan'), or add constraints.

Advanced techniques: prompt chaining (feed outputs into the next prompt), chain-of-thought (ask for step-by-step reasoning), tree-of-thought (explore multiple paths), and designing AI agents with personas.
Use AI responsibly: check outputs for accuracy, bias and hallucinations, and keep a human in the loop.
w5d2n1: Prompt injection is when user input overrides a developer's instructions in a prompt. It works because a language model reads everything as one block of text and can't reliably tell trusted instructions from untrusted input.

Four types: direct (the user types something like 'ignore the above and…'), indirect (instructions hidden in a web page or document the AI reads), code injection (tricking an AI into writing or running harmful code) and recursive (one model's output carries instructions into a second model).
Example: an app that pastes user input into a 'write a story about…' template can be told to ignore the template, because models often follow the most recent or most specific instruction.
Real case: users hijacked remoteli.io's Twitter bot by putting instructions in their tweets. It went viral and the company shut the bot down.
Risks include leaked system prompts or private data, malware generation, misinformation and exposed API keys. There is no complete fix yet, so AI products need layered defences.
w3d3r2: One-line prompts to AI app builders like Bolt and Lovable give mediocre results. Generating a PRD first can improve output dramatically.
Step 1: ask a reasoning model (Grok in Think mode, or ChatGPT o3/o4-mini) for a PRD covering product overview, target users, user stories, functional requirements and success metrics.
Include specifics in the prompt, such as the tech stack (e.g. React) and the core idea (an app for dentists to schedule patient appointments).
Step 2: review and edit the PRD, then paste the whole thing into Bolt or Lovable as the build prompt.
Result: a much more complete first version, with features, pages and flows matching the requirements, and fewer follow-up fixes.
w3d4r1: Visily is an AI-powered wireframing tool. Its AI features live in the left-side AI panel.
Screenshot to Design converts screenshots of existing apps into editable wireframes (also via the Chrome extension). Sketch to Design turns hand-drawn sketches into wireframes.
Text to Diagram creates diagrams from a description. The lo-fi/hi-fi switcher lets you validate core functionality in low fidelity, then polish in high fidelity.
Magic Theme extracts color themes from a website or image. Magic Image generates matching visuals from a description.
Smart Table Data Fill populates tables with realistic data (names, addresses, phone numbers) so mockups look complete.
w3d4r2: Visily's Text to Design turns a prompt (e.g. 'a mobile CRM app with a dashboard, account view and attached documents') into multiple screens in about 90 seconds.
Auto Prototyping also generates the connections between screens, so you can click through the prototype immediately.
Everything stays editable. Fix a missing link (e.g. a broken back button) or adjust designs by hand.
The point: AI automates time-consuming but low-thinking work (wiring obvious connections), so PMs and designers spend their time conveying ideas.
w5d3n1: Marina Danilevsky (IBM Research): on their own, LLMs answer from what they learned in training, so they can be confidently wrong, out of date and unable to cite a source.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) adds a content store, such as the web or a company's own documents. Before answering, the system first retrieves information relevant to the question.
The prompt then combines three things: instructions, the retrieved content and the user's question. The model answers from that evidence and can point to where it came from.
To keep answers current, you update the content store instead of retraining the model. Grounding also reduces made-up answers and lets the model say 'I don't know'.
The weak point is retrieval: if the right content isn't found, a question that could be answered goes unanswered, so teams work on improving both retrieval and generation.
w5d3n2: Product School: RAG connects a language model to trusted, up-to-date sources at the moment of asking, so it doesn't need retraining every time the information changes.

How it works: documents are split into chunks, turned into embeddings (numbers that capture meaning) and stored in a vector database. At query time the closest chunks are found and added to the prompt.

For PMs, it's usually a faster and cheaper way to make AI work with company knowledge than fine-tuning. Examples include Intercom's Fin for support, Glean for workplace search and AI-written sales emails.
Benefits: more accurate, current answers, fewer made-up facts, the ability to cite sources, and tighter control over which data the AI can see.
Risks to plan for: messy source data, poor chunking, vague questions, slow responses, privacy and licensing. A key PM question for any AI feature is 'where does its knowledge come from?'
w5d3n3: Maya Murad (IBM): AI is moving from single models to 'compound AI systems', where a model is combined with other parts like databases, search and code.
A model alone can't answer 'how many vacation days do I have?' because it can't see your records. A system that lets the model query the HR database can.
Most systems follow a fixed path set by the programmer (RAG is a common example). An agent puts the LLM in charge of deciding the path: it plans, acts and adjusts.
